paras: The threatened lynching of Sam Haines was a manhunt in June 1888 at a place printed as 'Rochville' or 'Rochvine', reported from Atlanta, Georgia, after Haines, a Black man, was accused of killing his wife and their two-day-old child. A search party of both white and Black men pursued him, and the dispatch said he would be lynched when found. No report of his capture or of a lynching appears in the coverage.

According to a special dispatch from Atlanta dated June 11, Haines, described as 'colored', killed his wife and a two-days-old child that morning while drunk. He then fled. The dispatch reported that 'a party of both whites and blacks' was looking for him and stated, without attributing the intention to anyone, that 'When found he will be lynched.' It named no officers and gave no size for the party.

No later report was found of Haines being caught, arrested, tried or lynched, and no inquest into the deaths of his wife and child appears in the coverage. The place name itself is uncertain: the item was set twice in overlapping form, once as 'Rochville' and once as 'Rochvine', and no county is given.

The only report found ran on June 14, 1888, on the front page of the Stark County Democrat of Canton, Ohio, as one of a column of brief telegraphic 'Specials' from across the country. Placed between a Uniontown, Pennsylvania, robbery and a bulletin on General Sheridan's health, the two-sentence item carried no headline of its own. It treated the coming lynching as a matter of course, stating it as a forecast rather than a rumor and offering no comment on it. Its note that the hunters were both white and Black was the only detail it gave about them. No account of the episode in a Georgia paper was found.

A1 reports only a threat ('When found he will be lynched') by a search party acting on a murder accusation; no report of Haines being caught or killed was found, so as reported this is a threatened lynching, not a completed one (A1).
One brief Atlanta special printed in one Ohio paper is the only report found (A1).

accounts.label: Atlanta special dispatch
accounts.gist: Haines, drunk, killed his wife and two-days-old child, fled, and was being hunted by a party of whites and blacks who would lynch him when found.

framing.detail: An undisplayed Atlanta 'Special' in a column of national briefs; the lynching is forecast flatly ('When found he will be lynched') with no comment.

conflicts.note: The item is printed twice in overlapping form (a doubled line); the two spellings are probably the same place garbled by typesetting or OCR. Neither matches 'Rockville' exactly.

record_check.dossier: threatened: the party was searching and said to intend lynching; no attempt on Haines is reported
printed 'Rochville'/'Rochvine'; Rockville is a plausible reading but not printed
no county named in the coverage
Georgia inferred from the Atlanta, Ga., dateline
a 'party of both whites and blacks'; no officers or deputizing mentioned

info: The morning of June 11, 1888 (dispatch dated Atlanta, June 11, says 'this morning').
Printed 'Rochville' and, in a repeated line, 'Rochvine'; no county is named.
Sam Haines, described as 'colored', was the man the search party threatened to lynch; his wife and a two-days-old child, unnamed, were the people he was accused of killing.
Accused of killing his wife and a two-days-old child while drunk.
'A party of both whites and blacks' searching for Haines.
Haines had fled and was still at large when the dispatch was sent; no later report of capture, lynching or arrest was found.

sources.note: Atlanta, Ga., June 11 special in a column of telegraphic briefs: Sam Haines, colored, while drunk killed his wife and a two-days-old child at 'Rochville'/'Rochvine', fled; a party of whites and blacks hunting him; 'When found he will be lynched.'
quotes: At Rochvine this morning Sam Haines, colored, while drunk killed his wife and a two-days-old child. He fled.
